# Episodic & External Memory Systems {#sec-vol3-episodic-memory}

Autonomous agency requires reasoning across temporal horizons that extend far beyond the physical boundaries of a single GPU context window. While volatile working memory and virtual paging substrates preserve intra-trajectory token activations, long-horizon software and digital agents must retain durable knowledge, operational heuristics, and causal environmental states across thousands of independent execution turns, tool failures, and process restarts. Treating the context window as an unbounded append-only log triggers catastrophic prefill latency penalties, exhausts high-bandwidth accelerator memory, and induces attention dispersion. Conversely, naive offloading to external vector databases introduces polarity blindness, structural amnesia over code syntax, and context poisoning from stale environmental observations. Sustaining reliable autonomous execution over months-long lifecycles mandates engineering a multi-tier memory hierarchy—spanning volatile context registers, dense metric index spaces, symbolic entity graphs, and transactional belief ledgers—governed by strict write-ahead consistency boundaries, offline consolidation cycles, and rigorous retrieval latency budgets.

## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

_How does an agent retain durable knowledge across trajectories without poisoning its working set?_

Without a durable external memory tier, an autonomous agent's operational lifetime is strictly bounded by the physical capacity of its accelerator context window, causing catastrophic forgetting of critical execution discoveries once the active token buffer is recycled. Yet simply dumping unstructured execution logs into a vector database introduces severe failure modes: high-dimensional embeddings suffer from polarity blindness, where catastrophic failure traces and successful completions cluster identically, while naive text chunking shatters the deterministic syntax of code and dependency graphs. Overcoming these fundamental limits requires engineering a strict transactional boundary between volatile GPU context and persistent secondary storage, implementing hybrid graph-vector topologies to guarantee structural recall, deploying temporal truth maintenance systems to continuously resolve factual contradictions in non-stationary environments, and bounding retrieval overheads within sub-second Service Level Agreements (SLAs). In agentic systems, the runtime must co-design the neural policy proposal engine with deterministic external storage boundaries.

## The Memory Hierarchy: From Registers to Secondary Storage {#sec-vol3-episodic-hierarchy}

An autonomous site-reliability engineering agent is deployed to resolve an intermittent deadlock across a Kubernetes-orchestrated payments cluster. Over four hours and 140 sequential turns, the agent inspects container logs, parses configuration maps, queries Prometheus metrics, and isolates a race condition between a Redis cache invalidation webhook and a PostgreSQL write replica. At turn 141, an infrastructure host node crashes due to an out-of-memory (OOM) event on an adjacent pod. When the agent process restarts on a healthy node, its entire context window and volatile Key-Value (KV) cache are gone. Rehydrating from turn zero with only the initial user prompt, the agent has forgotten all 140 turns of investigative findings. It begins re-executing its initial diagnostic scripts, re-probes the database, triggers the identical race condition, and drops the payment replica a second time.

This failure reveals the cost of conflating active reasoning context with durable memory. In classical computer architecture, memory systems balance access latency against storage capacity across a strict physical hierarchy: fast, expensive registers and SRAM caches sit adjacent to the arithmetic logic units, backed by larger, slower DRAM, which is in turn paged to non-volatile secondary storage [@hennessy2011computer; @saltzer2009]. An autonomous machine learning system requires an analogous storage hierarchy to decouple transient execution state from durable operational knowledge.

### The tripartite memory abstraction

When translated into the systems architecture of autonomous AI agents, memory partitions across three functional tiers:

1. **Parametric Memory ($\theta$):** The frozen weights of the underlying transformer foundation model [@vaswani2017], acquired through expensive pretraining and reinforcement learning runs (@sec-vol3-sft). Parametric memory contains generalized reasoning heuristics, language syntax, and world knowledge, but remains strictly immutable during inference.
2. **Volatile Context Memory (Working Set):** The active prompt buffer and its corresponding Key-Value (KV) activation tensors mapped into GPU High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) and host DRAM (@sec-vol3-virtual-memory). Context memory acts as the agent's CPU register file and L1/L2 cache—ultra-low latency, highly scarce, and fundamentally volatile.
3. **Non-Volatile Episodic Memory (Persistent Storage):** External, append-only, indexed secondary storage that captures the agent's historical trajectory epochs, raw tool execution traces, environmental diffs, and intermediate reflections across unbounded operational horizons.

Just as classical operating systems cannot execute programs without virtual memory and persistent block devices [@silberschatz2018; @denning1970], autonomous agents cannot sustain complex, multi-turn reasoning workflows without an episodic storage tier. Without episodic memory, an agent's operational lifetime is strictly bounded by the physical capacity of its context window ($N_{\max}$). When context overflows, older observations are truncated or summarized, discarding deterministic historical facts and triggering catastrophic forgetting.

### Physical characteristics across storage tiers

Each tier in the agent memory hierarchy exhibits distinct trade-offs across latency, bandwidth, capacity, cost, and durability invariants, as summarized in @tbl-vol3-episodic-memory-hierarchy.

| **L2: Paged KV Cache**     | Host DRAM / CXL                    | 1M – 10M tokens         | 10 – 50 ms (Swap)                    | 100 – 400 GB/s                    | Volatile (Node-bound)    | Medium (~\$5/GB)    |

L1 Context Registers provide instantaneous access during the transformer forward pass, but cost thousands of dollars in capital expenditure per terabyte and lose all state upon process termination. L2 Paged KV Cache expands volatile capacity across host memory via PagedAttention and CXL interconnects (@sec-vol3-virtual-memory), but remains node-bound and vulnerable to machine reboots. The L3 Episodic tier trades nanosecond memory bus access for durable, petabyte-scale persistence over local NVMe arrays and distributed network backends.

### Transaction boundaries and the write-ahead log invariant

When an agent executes an operational trajectory $\tau = (s_0, a_0, o_0, s_1, a_1, o_1, \dots, s_T)$, each step mutates two independent state domains:

1. **Internal Cognitive State ($\mathcal{S}_{\text{agent}}$):** The volatile sequence of tokens in the prompt buffer, attention KV-cache tensors in GPU HBM, and local execution variables.
2. **External Environmental State ($\mathcal{S}_{\text{env}}$):** The state of the physical or digital execution environment, including file systems, cloud infrastructure APIs, database rows, and git repositories.

A critical systems failure occurs when an agent crashes mid-trajectory—due to a network timeout, an out-of-memory kill on the model server, or a hardware fault. If the runtime fails to enforce strict transaction boundaries, the agent rehydrates in an inconsistent state: it may re-execute irreversible external tool actions (such as dispatching duplicate financial transactions or dropping database tables twice), or it may retain hallucinated beliefs about actions that never physically committed.

To prevent state divergence, production agent runtimes adopt the transactional foundations formalized by Jim Gray [@gray1981transaction]:

- **Atomicity:** An agent's tool execution and its corresponding state update must either complete fully or leave the environment unmodified.
- **Consistency:** An observation appended to episodic memory must satisfy environmental validation invariants, such as schema conformance and valid exit codes.
- **Isolation:** Concurrent agent threads operating on shared repositories must not read uncommitted or partial tool outputs from peer agents.
- **Durability:** Once an action-observation tuple $(a_t, o_t)$ is logged to episodic memory, it must survive catastrophic crashes of the runtime host.

In classical database engines, the Write-Ahead Log (WAL) protocol enforces the rule that no data page shall be written to non-volatile storage until the log record describing the update has been flushed to disk [@gray1978notes; @mohan1992aries]. For an autonomous agent runtime mutating external systems, this invariant must be inverted and hardened:

$$\text{Log}(s_t, a_t) \prec_{\text{commit}} \text{Execute}(a_t) \prec_{\text{commit}} \text{Log}(o_t, s_{t+1}) $$

where $\prec_{\text{commit}}$ denotes strict serial precedence enforced by a synchronous `fsync` storage barrier.

As shown in @fig-vol3-episodic-wal-flow, the agent runtime must never dispatch an external tool command $a_t$ across the actuation boundary until the proposed action and current working state $s_t$ have been persisted to a local append-only log. If the host crashes while $a_t$ is executing, the rehydration engine parses the log tail, discovers an uncompleted action record, and initiates recovery routines (@sec-vol3-checkpointing) rather than blindly re-invoking the action.

### Agent sleep lifecycle and rehydration

Maintaining an agent's working context in active GPU HBM while it waits for long-running external operations incurs severe financial and operational waste. When an agent invokes a tool that compiles a large C++ codebase, awaits human authorization, or polls a continuous integration pipeline, the task blocks on I/O for seconds, minutes, or hours. If the serving runtime pins the KV cache in accelerator memory throughout this interval, it incurs the **Tool-Wait Memory Tax**\index{Tool-Wait Memory Tax}, stranding tens of gigabytes of premium HBM while tensor cores sit idle.

Persistent episodic memory resolves this through the **Agent Sleep Lifecycle**\index{Agent Sleep Lifecycle}:

1. **Eviction and Sleep Transition:** When an agent yields execution to await an asynchronous event, the runtime serializes its execution context:
   - The token sequence and active system prompts are appended to the episodic event ledger.
   - Paged KV cache blocks are released via `munmap` and returned to the accelerator memory pool.
   - The Agent Control Block (ACB)—including active tool descriptors, scratchpad variables, and Lamport logical timestamps—is persisted to disk.
   - The execution container terminates or transitions to an idle event-wait state.
2. **Rehydration and Wake Transition:** Upon receiving an event trigger (such as a webhook callback or CI build completion), the agent rehydrates:
   - An available container instance allocates execution resources.
   - The runtime reconstructs the working set by fetching the latest checkpoint snapshot and tail log records from the episodic store.
   - Prefix KV caching warms invariant system prompts in millisecond latency, restoring the agent to its exact cognitive state without quadratic recomputation.

With the physical storage hierarchy and transactional persistence boundaries established, the primary systems challenge shifts from durability to retrieval. Storing terabytes of historical context is futile if the agent cannot locate relevant observations within millisecond latency budgets.

## Vector Indices and Approximate Nearest Neighbor Systems {#sec-vol3-episodic-vector-ann}

An autonomous code migration agent processes a 200,000-line legacy Java repository into Go. Over 300 execution turns, it writes 45,000 episodic logs containing compiler errors, AST diffs, and terminal outputs. When tasked with fixing an `AbstractMethodError`, the agent queries its episodic vector database using brute-force exact cosine search over $D=1536$ dimensional FP32 embeddings. The search requires evaluating $45,000 \times 1536$ multiply-accumulate operations per query, consuming 275 ms on the CPU host. As the repository history swells to 1.5 million vectors over two weeks of migration, query latency explodes to 9.2 seconds per tool turn. The agent spends 80 percent of its execution time waiting for vector distance calculations, stalling the actuation loop. When an engineer switches to naive spatial $k$-d trees, query latency actually gets worse due to the curse of dimensionality.

Unstructured episodic text—including terminal logs, compiler traces, and free-form intermediate thoughts—lacks explicit relational schemas. Dense vector retrieval maps these unstructured strings into continuous embedding spaces where geometric proximity models semantic relatedness. However, scaling vector retrieval to millions of historical trajectory tokens requires overcoming fundamental computational and geometric bottlenecks in high-dimensional metric spaces.

### High-dimensional metric topologies

In an episodic store, observation strings $x \in \mathcal{X}$ are mapped into a dense continuous vector space by an embedding encoder $f_\phi: \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}^D$:

$$\mathbf{v} = \frac{f_\phi(x)}{\|f_\phi(x)\|_2} $$

Normalizing vectors to unit length ($\|\mathbf{v}\|_2 = 1$) simplifies cosine similarity to an inner product:

$$S_C(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{v}) = \frac{\mathbf{q} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{q}\|_2 \|\mathbf{v}\|_2} = \mathbf{q}^T \mathbf{v} $$

Under unit normalization, maximizing cosine similarity is mathematically equivalent to minimizing squared Euclidean distance:

$$\|\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{v}\|_2^2 = \|\mathbf{q}\|_2^2 + \|\mathbf{v}\|_2^2 - 2 \mathbf{q}^T \mathbf{v} = 2(1 - S_C(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{v})) $$

Exact nearest neighbor search across $N$ stored vectors requires computing $N$ inner products of dimension $D$, demanding $2 \cdot N \cdot D$ floating-point operations (FLOPs). For an episodic store with $N = 10^7$ memories and $D = 1536$, a single query requires over $30.7\text{ GFLOPs}$. On a modern multi-core CPU with a memory bandwidth of $B_{\text{mem}} = 100\text{ GB/s}$, streaming the raw vectors ($10^7 \times 1536 \times 4\text{ bytes} \approx 61.4\text{ GB}$) imposes a physical latency floor of:

$$T_{\text{exact\_scan}} = \frac{61.4\text{ GB}}{100\text{ GB/s}} \approx 614\text{ ms} $$

A 614 ms memory scan per tool turn violates interactive execution budgets.

### The curse of dimensionality

Attempting to accelerate spatial search using classical partitioning trees (such as $k$-d trees or $R$-trees) fails catastrophically in high-dimensional embedding spaces due to the **Curse of Dimensionality**\index{Curse of Dimensionality}.

As formalized by @beyer1999nearest, for independent and identically distributed random vectors in high dimensions, the distance contrast between the nearest and farthest neighbors vanishes:

$$\lim_{D \to \infty} \frac{\max_{1 \le i \le N} \|\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{q}\|_p - \min_{1 \le i \le N} \|\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{q}\|_p}{\min_{1 \le i \le N} \|\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{q}\|_p} = 0 $$

This loss of contrast stems from the geometry of high-dimensional hyperspheres. The volume of a $D$-dimensional hypersphere of radius $r$ is:

$$V_D(r) = \frac{\pi^{D/2}}{\Gamma(D/2 + 1)} r^D $$

The fraction of volume contained in a thin outer shell of thickness $\epsilon \cdot r$ (where $0 < \epsilon < 1$) is:

$$\frac{V_D(r) - V_D(r(1 - \epsilon))}{V_D(r)} = 1 - (1 - \epsilon)^D $$

For $D = 1536$ and $\epsilon = 0.01$, this ratio evaluates to $1 - (0.99)^{1536} \approx 1 - 1.9 \times 10^{-7} \approx 0.9999998$. Virtually $100\%$ of the volume resides within the outermost $1\%$ shell of the hypersphere. Because all points are approximately equidistant from each other, spatial bounding boxes overlap across every partition, forcing spatial trees to inspect every branch and degenerating into an exhaustive $O(N \cdot D)$ linear scan.

To achieve sub-millisecond retrieval across millions of memories, agent architectures must employ **Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN)**\index{Approximate Nearest Neighbor} indexing, trading exact distance guarantees for orders-of-magnitude speedups.

### Inverted file product quantization (IVF-PQ) and ADC

For memory-constrained episodic runtimes, **Inverted File Product Quantization (IVF-PQ)**\index{Inverted File Product Quantization (IVF-PQ)} [@jegou2011product] combines spatial clustering with lossy sub-vector compression:

1. **Inverted File (IVF) Coarse Partitioning:** The vector space is partitioned into $K_{\text{ivf}}$ Voronoi cells using $k$-means clustering over centroids $\{\mathbf{c}_1, \dots, \mathbf{c}_{K_{\text{ivf}}}\}$. At query time, the search engine computes distances only to the nearest $n_{\text{probe}} \ll K_{\text{ivf}}$ centroids, pruning $(1 - n_{\text{probe}} / K_{\text{ivf}})$ of the candidate vectors from consideration.
2. **Product Quantization (PQ):** Instead of storing raw high-dimensional residual vectors $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{c}_i$, the residual is split into $M$ orthogonal sub-vectors of dimension $d^* = D / M$:
   $$\mathbf{r} = [\mathbf{r}^{(1)}, \mathbf{r}^{(2)}, \dots, \mathbf{r}^{(M)}], \quad \mathbf{r}^{(m)} \in \mathbb{R}^{d^*} $$
   Each sub-vector space is quantized using a codebook of $K_{\text{pq}} = 256$ centroids. Because $256 = 2^8$, each sub-vector is represented by an 8-bit byte index. A 1536-dimensional FP32 vector (requiring 6,144 bytes) is compressed into $M$ bytes. For $M = 64$, this achieves a **$96\times$ compression factor**, reducing the memory footprint of $10^7$ vectors from $61.4\text{ GB}$ to $640\text{ MB}$, allowing the entire index to reside permanently in host RAM.

3. **Asymmetric Distance Computation (ADC):** During search, the query vector $\mathbf{q}$ is *not* quantized. The runtime precomputes a distance lookup table $\mathcal{D} \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times 256}$ storing the squared Euclidean distance between each query sub-vector and each codebook centroid:
   $$\mathcal{D}[m, k] = \|\mathbf{q}^{(m)} - \mathbf{c}_k^{(m)}\|^2, \quad \forall m \in \{1, \dots, M\}, \ k \in \{0, \dots, 255\} $$
   Computing $\mathcal{D}$ requires only $M \times 256 \times d^* = 256 \cdot D$ multiply-accumulate operations—a negligible constant overhead (e.g., $393\text{ kFLOPs}$ for $D=1536$). The table consumes $64 \times 256 \times 4\text{ bytes} = 64\text{ KB}$, fitting entirely within the CPU's L1/L2 data cache.

The distance between the query and any stored quantized vector $\mathbf{x}$ is evaluated via:

$$d_{\text{ADC}}(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{x}) = \sum_{m=1}^M \mathcal{D}[m, k_m(\mathbf{x})] $$ {#eq-vol3-episodic-adc}

Evaluating @eq-vol3-episodic-adc requires exactly $M$ array lookups and $M-1$ scalar additions—zero floating-point multiplications during index traversal.

Residual vectors are sliced into $M$ sub-vectors and quantized to centroid codes. During query execution, unquantized query vector $\mathbf{q}$ evaluates exact distances to sub-codebooks, constructing a lookup table for $O(1)$ Asymmetric Distance Computation (ADC) across postings lists. ### Graph-based proximity navigation (HNSW)

Where IVF-PQ optimizes memory footprint through lossy compression, **Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW)**\index{Hierarchical Navigable Small World} graphs optimize query latency and recall by constructing multi-layer geometric proximity graphs [@malkov2020hnsw].

Inspired by skip-lists, an HNSW index builds a hierarchy of graph layers $\ell \in \{0, 1, \dots, L_{\max}\}$. Layer 0 contains every stored vector as a vertex, with edges connecting nearest neighbors according to a heuristic that balances proximity with directional diversity. Each superior layer contains an exponentially decaying subset of vertices, selected with probability:

$$P(\text{level} \ge \ell) = \exp(-\ell / m_L), \quad m_L = \frac{1}{\ln(M_{\text{hnsw}})} $$

where $M_{\text{hnsw}}$ governs the maximum number of bidirectional connections per node. The uppermost layers contain sparse, long-range "highway" edges that allow greedy search to traverse vast geometric distances in single hops, achieving logarithmic routing complexity:

$$\mathcal{O}(\log N) $$

Query routing proceeds greedily from top to bottom:

1. Search begins at a global entry point at the topmost layer $L_{\max}$.
2. The algorithm evaluates distances to all graph neighbors of the current vertex, stepping greedily to whichever neighbor is closest to the query $\mathbf{q}$.
3. When a local minimum is reached in layer $\ell$, the search drops to the corresponding vertex in layer $\ell - 1$.
4. Upon reaching Layer 0, the algorithm executes an expanded beam search of size $efSearch$, returning the top-$k$ nearest neighbors.

While HNSW achieves superior recall (>98 percent) and sub-millisecond query latency ($< 2\text{ ms}$), its memory footprint is substantial. Storing $M_{\text{hnsw}} = 32$ to $64$ bidirectional integer pointers per vector alongside uncompressed 1536-dimensional FP32 vectors consumes:

$$S_{\text{HNSW}} = N \times (D \cdot 4 + 2 \cdot M_{\text{hnsw}} \cdot 8) \approx 6,144 + 1,024 = 7,168\text{ bytes/vector} $$

For $10^7$ memories, HNSW demands over $71\text{ GB}$ of resident RAM, requiring dedicated memory-optimized nodes.

### Polarity blindness and the limits of cosine geometry

Despite their speed, dense vector stores exhibit an architectural failure mode that frequently derails autonomous agent reasoning: **Polarity Blindness**\index{Polarity Blindness}.

Standard embedding models are trained using contrastive objective functions, such as InfoNCE:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{InfoNCE}} = -\log \frac{\exp(\mathbf{q} \cdot \mathbf{k}^+ / \tau)}{\exp(\mathbf{q} \cdot \mathbf{k}^+ / \tau) + \sum_{j} \exp(\mathbf{q} \cdot \mathbf{k}_j^- / \tau)} $$

Because the loss penalizes topical dissimilarity, sentences sharing identical technical subjects, entities, and syntactic vocabulary project to adjacent points in latent space—even if their truth values are diametrically opposed.

Listing @lst-vol3-episodic-polarity-blindness demonstrates this failure mode using concrete sentence pairs.

::: {#lst-vol3-episodic-polarity-blindness lst-cap="**Demonstration of Polarity Blindness in Dense Embeddings**: High cosine similarity between contradictory propositions compared to an unrelated topical control."}
```python
import numpy as np

def cosine_similarity(u: np.ndarray, v: np.ndarray) -> float:
    return float(np.dot(u, v) / (np.linalg.norm(u) * np.linalg.norm(v)))

# Conceptual embeddings from standard contrastive encoders
# s1: Execution success record
# s2: Catastrophic execution failure record
# s3: Unrelated topical control
s1_text = "Database migration script 042 executed successfully with zero errors."
s2_text = "Database migration script 042 failed catastrophically with fatal syntax errors."
s3_text = "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy sleeping dog."

# Representative high-dimensional cosine similarity evaluation:
# S_C(s1, s2) = 0.942  <-- High similarity despite opposite factual reality!
# S_C(s1, s3) = 0.087
```
:::

If an agent queries its episodic memory with: *"Did database migration 042 succeed?"*, an ANN search returns both the success log and the fatal failure log with nearly indistinguishable similarity scores ($S_C \approx 0.94$). If the prompt assembly engine blindly injects the top candidate, the agent risks consuming an obsolete error traceback or a negated premise.

Dense latent spaces encode **thematic affinity**, not **propositional truth**. Systems requiring deterministic factual correctness cannot rely solely on vector proximity; they must ground retrieval in structured representations that capture the exact relational topology of the environment.

## Knowledge Graphs and Symbolic Relational Stores {#sec-vol3-episodic-graphs}

An autonomous agent is tasked with upgrading an API gateway across a distributed architecture of 35 microservices. The engineer asks the agent to evaluate the blast radius of modifying `AuthService.validate_session()`. The agent issues an ANN vector search for "services calling validate_session". The vector index retrieves 10 docstrings from services that happen to contain the word "validate_session", but completely misses two critical billing services that invoke the method through an inherited base class `SessionAuthenticator`. Concluding that billing is unaffected, the agent applies the breaking change, instantly causing an outage in the subscription processing pipeline.

When an agent operates over structured, deterministic environments—such as code repositories, microservice meshes, and cloud infrastructure topologies—unstructured text chunking fails. Dividing source code into arbitrary 512-token segments shatters class inheritance hierarchies, severs function call sites from their definitions, and discards static typing constraints. Capturing structural dependencies requires compiling execution environments into **Symbolic Knowledge Graphs**\index{Symbolic Knowledge Graphs} and relational stores.

### Tree-Sitter AST skeletonization

The foundation of code-aware episodic memory is grammar-based structural parsing via **Tree-Sitter**\index{Tree-Sitter}, an incremental, concrete syntax tree (CST) parser generator.

Rather than splitting source files by token count, the episodic indexing engine parses source code into syntax trees. It then executes structural queries to prune implementation bodies, retaining only the symbol interface skeleton:

- Module import declarations and external package dependencies
- Class declarations, base class inheritance lists, and type parameters
- Method signatures, parameter types, return types, and docstrings
- Exported constants, interface contracts, and schema definitions

Pruning implementation bodies discards 90 to 95 percent of raw code tokens while preserving 100 percent of symbol names and interface boundaries.

Listing @lst-vol3-episodic-tree-sitter-skeleton illustrates AST skeletonization using Python's native syntax grammar.

::: {#lst-vol3-episodic-tree-sitter-skeleton lst-cap="**Incremental AST Skeletonization**: Discarding implementation bodies while preserving typed symbol signatures and interface declarations."}
```python
import ast

def skeletonize_python_source(source_code: str) -> str:
    """Prune function and method bodies to minimize token footprint

    while preserving complete structural interface contracts.
    """
    tree = ast.parse(source_code)
    for node in ast.walk(tree):
        if isinstance(node, (ast.FunctionDef, ast.AsyncFunctionDef)):
            # Preserve docstring if present, replace body with Ellipsis (...)
            docstring = ast.get_docstring(node)
            new_body = []
            if docstring:
                new_body.append(ast.Expr(value=ast.Constant(value=docstring)))
            new_body.append(ast.Expr(value=ast.Constant(value=Ellipsis)))
            node.body = new_body
    return ast.unparse(tree)
```
:::

The token reduction ratio achieved by skeletonization is parameterized as:

$$\rho_{\text{prune}} = 1 - \frac{T_{\text{skeleton}}}{T_{\text{full}}} $$

In production software repositories, $\rho_{\text{prune}}$ typically ranges between $0.90$ and $0.95$. A 500,000-token repository compresses into an interface skeleton of 25,000 to 50,000 tokens, enabling structural symbol maps to fit directly within long-context prompts.

### Symbol dependency graphs and personalized PageRank

From the extracted AST skeletons, the runtime constructs a directed **Symbol Dependency Graph**\index{Symbol Dependency Graph} $G = (V, E)$:

- **Vertices ($V$):** Every uniquely qualified symbol in the codebase (e.g., `services.auth.TokenValidator.verify_jwt`).
- **Edges ($E$):** Directed relationships between symbols, categorized by type:
  - $\text{Defines}(f, s)$: File $f$ defines symbol $s$.
  - $\text{Calls}(s_1, s_2)$: Symbol $s_1$ invokes function or method $s_2$.
  - $\text{Inherits}(c_1, c_2)$: Class $c_1$ extends base class $c_2$.
  - $\text{Imports}(f, m)$: File $f$ imports module $m$.

When an agent modifies a specific function or debugs an error traceback, injecting the entire repository graph into the context window exceeds token budgets. The runtime must select the subset of symbols most topologically relevant to the agent's current focus.

To accomplish this, the system executes **Personalized PageRank (PPR)**\index{Personalized PageRank} [@page1999pagerank] over the symbol graph. Unlike standard PageRank, which models a random walk with uniform teleportation probability across all nodes, Personalized PageRank teleports exclusively to a designated set of **seed vertices** $\mathcal{S} \subset V$—such as the files or functions currently open or edited by the agent:

$$\mathbf{p}^{(t+1)} = (1 - \alpha) \mathbf{P}^T \mathbf{p}^{(t)} + \alpha \mathbf{s} $$

where:

- $\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{D}^{-1} \mathbf{A}$ is the row-stochastic transition probability matrix derived from graph adjacency matrix $\mathbf{A}$.
- $\alpha \in [0.15, 0.20]$ is the teleportation (restart) probability.
- $\mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^{|V|}$ is the personalization vector, with $s_i = 1 / |\mathcal{S}|$ if $i \in \mathcal{S}$, and $s_i = 0$ otherwise.

The stationary distribution $\mathbf{p}^* = \lim_{t \to \infty} \mathbf{p}^{(t)}$ satisfies:

$$\mathbf{p}^* = \alpha [\mathbf{I} - (1 - \alpha) \mathbf{P}^T]^{-1} \mathbf{s} $$

The stationary probability $p_v^*$ quantifies the structural relevance of symbol $v$ relative to the active seed set $\mathcal{S}$.

### Knapsack context packing

Given the relevance scores $p_v^*$ and token costs $\text{cost}(v)$ for each skeletonized symbol, the runtime selects the optimal context set within a designated repomap token budget $B_{\text{repomap}}$ by formulating a 0-1 Knapsack Problem:

$$\max \sum_{v \in V} p_v^* \cdot x_v \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \sum_{v \in V} \text{cost}(v) \cdot x_v \le B_{\text{repomap}}, \quad x_v \in \{0, 1\} $$ {#eq-vol3-episodic-knapsack}

Because the 0-1 knapsack problem is NP-complete, the runtime uses a greedy approximation that sorts symbols by score density $p_v^* / \text{cost}(v)$ and packs them until the budget is filled.

Listing @lst-vol3-episodic-ppr-knapsack implements Personalized PageRank computation and greedy knapsack packing.

::: {#lst-vol3-episodic-ppr-knapsack lst-cap="**Personalized PageRank and Knapsack Context Packing**: Iterative power-iteration PPR biased toward seed nodes, followed by greedy knapsack token packing."}
```python
import numpy as np

def compute_personalized_pagerank(
    adj_matrix: np.ndarray,
    seed_indices: list[int],
    alpha: float = 0.15,
    max_iter: int = 100,
    tol: float = 1e-6
) -> np.ndarray:
    """Compute stationary Personalized PageRank vector biased toward seeds."""
    n = adj_matrix.shape[0]
    out_degrees = adj_matrix.sum(axis=1)

    # Construct row-stochastic transition matrix P
    P = np.zeros_like(adj_matrix, dtype=float)
    nonzero = out_degrees > 0
    P[nonzero] = adj_matrix[nonzero] / out_degrees[nonzero, np.newaxis]
    P[~nonzero] = 1.0 / n  # Handle sink nodes

    # Personalization vector s
    s = np.zeros(n, dtype=float)
    s[seed_indices] = 1.0 / len(seed_indices)

    # Power iteration
    p = s.copy()
    for _ in range(max_iter):
        p_next = (1.0 - alpha) * np.dot(P.T, p) + alpha * s
        if np.linalg.norm(p_next - p, 1) < tol:
            break
        p = p_next
    return p

def pack_context_knapsack(
    symbols: list[str],
    scores: np.ndarray,
    token_costs: list[int],
    budget: int
) -> list[str]:
    """Greedy knapsack packing of symbols ordered by relevance density."""
    densities = [(scores[i] / token_costs[i], i) for i in range(len(symbols))]
    densities.sort(reverse=True, key=lambda x: x[0])

    selected_symbols = []
    total_tokens = 0
    for _, idx in densities:
        if total_tokens + token_costs[idx] <= budget:
            selected_symbols.append(symbols[idx])
            total_tokens += token_costs[idx]
    return selected_symbols
```
:::

### Relational SQL stores for deterministic state

While knowledge graphs capture topological relationships, exact operational attributes—such as tool return codes, execution timestamps, file hashes, and configuration parameters—require deterministic relational storage.

In an agent runtime, relational databases (e.g., PostgreSQL or SQLite) provide structured state queries that eliminate the fuzziness of vector search:

- Checking whether a specific migration script ran: `SELECT status FROM migrations WHERE id = 42;`
- Fetching active environment variables: `SELECT value FROM config WHERE key = 'DATABASE_URL';`
- Inspecting recent tool errors: `SELECT stdout, stderr FROM tool_executions WHERE exit_code != 0 ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 5;`

@Tbl-vol3-episodic-retrieval-modalities compares the four primary retrieval modalities in autonomous agent memory.

| Retrieval Modality          | Indexing Substrate                        | Primary Query Primitive                 | Semantic Resolution                     |             Token Density             | Critical Failure Mode                                 | Optimal Systems Role                                       |
|:----------------------------|:------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------:|:------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------|
| **Dense Vector Search**     | Continuous metric space ($\mathbb{R}^D$)  | Cosine similarity ($S_C$)               | Thematic affinity & fuzzy concepts      |  Low ($256\text{--}512$ tokens/chunk) | Polarity blindness; false positives on negated facts  | Broad exploratory recall; identifies seed entry points     |
| **Sparse Lexical Search**   | Inverted term index (BM25)                | Exact term frequency matching           | Lexical identity & token matching       |             Low to Medium             | Vocabulary mismatch; zero conceptual generalization   | Exact identifier lookups, compiler flags & error codes     |
| **Structural AST Repomap**  | Directed symbol graph $G=(V, E)$          | Personalized PageRank ($\mathbf{p}^*$)  | Syntactic callers, callees & interfaces | Exceptional ($95\%$ skeleton pruning) | Blind to dynamic dispatch & runtime reflection        | Deterministic code context; structural interface hydration |
| **Relational Event Ledger** | Append-only relational log (WAL / SQLite) | Relational SQL filter (`status = 'OK'`) | Propositional ground truth & timestamps |     High (Structured JSON records)    | Rigid schema; requires structured observation parsers | Authoritative belief state; audit replay & crash recovery  |

: **Comparison of Retrieval Modalities in Agent Episodic Memory**: Contrasting dense latent search, sparse lexical retrieval, structural AST graphs, and transactional ledgers across representations, query mechanisms, resolution, and systems failure modes. {#tbl-vol3-episodic-retrieval-modalities tbl-colwidths="[14,14,14,15,12,16,15]"}

### Hybrid graph-vector traversal pipelines

Because no single retrieval modality satisfies all operational requirements, production systems deploy a **Dual-Stage Hybrid Pipeline**\index{Dual-Stage Hybrid Pipeline}:

1. **Stage 1 (Latent Exploration):** The agent's query (e.g., *"Why is authentication timing out during token validation?"*) is embedded into latent space. ANN search retrieves the top-$k$ semantic code chunks and historical execution logs.
2. **Stage 2 (Topological Expansion):** The symbols identified in Stage 1 serve as the seed set $\mathcal{S}$ for Personalized PageRank over the repository symbol graph. Graph traversal propagates relevance across call graphs, inheritance edges, and import paths, pulling in dependent interface signatures that vector similarity missed.
3. **Stage 3 (Deterministic Context Packing):** The union of semantic chunks and graph skeletons is greedily packed into the prompt budget using @eq-vol3-episodic-knapsack.

This hybrid pipeline leverages dense vectors for initial entry-point discovery and graph topology for deterministic structural completeness.

## Memory Consolidation: Sleep Cycles, Summarization, and Reflection {#sec-vol3-episodic-consolidation}

An autonomous software maintenance agent is deployed in a continuous integration pipeline. Over five days, it processes 1,200 pull requests, logging 15 million raw execution tokens—including terminal tracebacks, bash diffs, compiler warnings, and rejected debugging hypotheses. By day six, the agent's episodic vector store is completely saturated with noisy, redundant observations. When asked to resolve an import conflict, the vector retrieval engine surfaces four contradictory, rejected hypotheses from three days earlier, confusing the agent into re-attempting an approach that had already been proven to cause circular import deadlocks. The agent enters an infinite retry loop, burning \$450 in API tokens before human engineers kill the process.

This degradation highlights the necessity of memory consolidation. In human neurobiology, memory relies on a dual-process architecture: the hippocampus captures high-frequency, raw episodic experiences during waking hours, while the neocortex slowly consolidates these traces into abstract semantic schemas during sleep cycles [@tulving1972episodic]. Autonomous agent runtimes require an analogous offline consolidation mechanism to distill raw execution trajectories into compact operational heuristics while eliminating obsolete beliefs.

### The agent sleep cycle architecture

Executing memory consolidation within an active agent's critical execution loop degrades responsiveness and multiplies token costs. Instead, production architectures implement **Offline Sleep Cycles**\index{Offline Sleep Cycles}:

1. **Trigger Conditions:** Sleep cycles execute asynchronously, triggered by:
   - **Temporal Schedules:** Low-traffic cron windows (e.g., nightly batch windows).
   - **Trajectory Boundaries:** Task completions or explicit milestone checkpoints.
   - **Memory Capacity Thresholds:** Accumulated uncompacted trajectory tokens exceeding a defined budget ($N_{\text{uncompacted}} \ge \Theta_{\text{mem}}$).
2. **Resource Isolation:** Consolidation jobs execute on auxiliary batch compute nodes (CPU clusters or lower-cost GPU pools), ensuring that background summarization never contends with active agent inference for accelerator memory bandwidth.

### Trajectory distillation and reflection

During a sleep cycle, the consolidation engine processes raw execution trajectories $\tau = (s_0, a_0, o_0, \dots, s_T)$ through a three-stage reflection architecture:

#### 1. Importance scoring

Every memory item $m$ in the episodic ledger is assigned an intrinsic importance score $I(m) \in [1, 10]$ evaluating its long-term operational value. High-importance items include fatal error post-mortems, architectural interface decisions, and user-specified constraints; low-importance items include transient directory listings and progress bar logs.

When evaluating memory items for reflection or retrieval, the runtime combines recency, importance, and query relevance:

$$\text{Score}(m, q) = w_{\text{rec}} \cdot \text{Recency}(m) + w_{\text{imp}} \cdot \frac{I(m)}{10} + w_{\text{rel}} \cdot S_C(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{v}_m) $$

where recency decays exponentially according to an elapsed-time decay constant $\lambda_{\text{decay}}$:

$$\text{Recency}(m) = \exp(-\lambda_{\text{decay}} \cdot (t_{\text{now}} - t_{\text{accessed}})) $$

#### 2. Generative reflection

The engine clusters recent memories with high importance scores and queries a background foundation model with meta-analytical reflection prompts:

- *"Given these 25 tool execution failures across the last 50 turns, what is the single underlying architectural defect causing them?"*
- *"Extract 3 durable procedural rules that must govern future database migrations based on these trajectory traces."*

The generated reflections represent high-order semantic abstractions. The runtime embeds these reflections and inserts them back into the episodic hierarchy as parent nodes linked to their underlying leaf observations.

#### 3. Trajectory distillation

Detailed trajectory turn sequences are compressed into canonical state-action summaries. The distillation compression ratio is defined as:

$$\mathcal{R}_{\text{distill}} = \frac{|\text{Tokens}_{\text{distilled}}|}{|\text{Tokens}_{\text{raw}}|} $$

In production runtimes, $\mathcal{R}_{\text{distill}}$ typically achieves values between $0.02$ and $0.05$—compressing raw trajectories by a factor of 20 to 50 while preserving causal operational lessons.

### Doyle's truth maintenance system (TMS)

In non-stationary environments, facts change: web services migrate, database schemas update, and configuration keys are renamed. A fatal defect in naive memory stores is retaining obsolete facts that contradict current reality.

To resolve contradictions systematically, agent episodic systems adapt Jon Doyle's classical **Truth Maintenance Systems (TMS)**\index{Truth Maintenance Systems} [@doyle1979truth].

In a TMS, every recorded belief atom is labeled as either:

- **$\text{IN}$:** Currently believed to be true (supported by active, uncontradicted evidence).
- **$\text{OUT}$:** Not currently believed (either lacking valid justification, retracted, or superseded by a newer observation).

Beliefs are connected through a directed justification network. When an agent executes an action that reveals an environmental change (e.g., discovering that a server listening on port 5432 has been remapped to port 5433), the TMS executes **Dependency-Directed Backtracking**\index{Dependency-Directed Backtracking}:

1. It identifies the belief asserting $\langle \texttt{PostgreSQL}, \texttt{port}, \texttt{5432} \rangle$.
2. It transitions that belief from $\text{IN}$ to $\text{OUT}$.
3. It recursively evaluates all downstream plans, hypotheses, or operational rules that relied on that belief as a premise, transitioning them to $\text{OUT}$.
4. It instantiates the new belief $\langle \texttt{PostgreSQL}, \texttt{port}, \texttt{5433} \rangle$ with status $\text{IN}$.

When the retrieval engine constructs context for the active prompt, it applies a strict invariant: **retrieve exclusively from the $\text{IN}$ partition**. Contradicted and obsolete observations are filtered at the storage boundary, eliminating temporal hallucinations before tokens enter the model's working set.

### Bi-temporal memory modeling

In enterprise systems, simply overwriting stale records with destructive `UPDATE` statements destroys historical auditability. If an autonomous agent triggers an outage, post-mortem telemetry engines (@sec-vol3-observability) must be able to reconstruct the exact cognitive state of the agent at the precise moment it dispatched the faulty command.

To achieve non-destructive belief updating with complete auditability, the episodic store adopts **Bi-Temporal Modeling**\index{Bi-Temporal Modeling} [@snodgrass1986temporal]. Every record tracks two independent temporal intervals:

1. **Valid Time ($T_V = [t_{v,\text{start}}, t_{v,\text{end}}]$):** The interval during which the assertion was true in the physical execution environment.
2. **Transaction Time ($T_T = [t_{t,\text{start}}, t_{t,\text{end}}]$):** The interval during which the assertion was stored and considered active within the agent's database.

Listing @lst-vol3-episodic-bitemporal-schema details the SQL schema for a bi-temporal belief ledger.

::: {#lst-vol3-episodic-bitemporal-schema lst-cap="**Bi-Temporal Episodic Memory Ledger Schema**: SQL schema supporting orthogonal Valid Time and Transaction Time intervals alongside Lamport logical clocks."}
```sql
CREATE TABLE episodic_belief_ledger (
    memory_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    agent_id UUID NOT NULL,
    entity VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    attribute VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    value JSONB NOT NULL,
    lamport_clock BIGINT NOT NULL,
    -- Valid Time: Reality interval
    valid_from TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE NOT NULL,
    valid_to TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE,
    -- Transaction Time: Storage interval
    tx_from TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    tx_to TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE,
    status VARCHAR(16) NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('IN', 'OUT'))
);

CREATE INDEX idx_active_beliefs ON episodic_belief_ledger (entity, attribute)
WHERE status = 'IN' AND valid_to IS NULL;
```
:::

When an update arrives, the existing record is not deleted or mutated in-place. Instead, its `valid_to` and `tx_to` timestamps are closed, and its status is updated to `OUT`. A new row is inserted asserting the new value with status `IN`.

This architecture enables two distinct query modes:

- **Active Execution Queries:**
  ```sql
  SELECT * FROM episodic_belief_ledger
  WHERE entity = 'PostgreSQL' AND status = 'IN' AND valid_to IS NULL;
  ```
- **Time-Travel Replay Queries (Point-in-Time Audit):**
  ```sql
  SELECT * FROM episodic_belief_ledger
  WHERE entity = 'PostgreSQL'
    AND valid_from <= '2026-09-10 14:00:00'
    AND (valid_to > '2026-09-10 14:00:00' OR valid_to IS NULL);
  ```

### Lamport logical clocks for distributed causal ordering

Relying on physical POSIX timestamps to order memories across distributed agent fleets introduces clock skew, NTP drift, and network reordering failures [@lamport1978time]. To enforce strict causal precedence, episodic memory records are stamped with **Lamport Logical Clocks**\index{Lamport Logical Clocks}:

- Each agent maintains a monotonic integer clock $L \in \mathbb{N}$, initialized to zero.
- Before executing an internal reasoning step or tool dispatch, the agent increments its local clock: $L \leftarrow L + 1$.
- Every message or tool payload carries the current timestamp $L_{\text{msg}}$.
- Upon receiving an external observation or peer message, the agent synchronizes its clock:
  $$L \leftarrow \max(L, L_{\text{msg}}) + 1 $$

Every memory item is indexed by the causal tuple $\langle \text{agent\_id}, L, \text{epoch} \rangle$, providing an unambiguous partial order over historical events regardless of physical clock drift.

@Tbl-vol3-episodic-temporal-paradigms compares these memory consistency paradigms.

| Consistency Paradigm                | Temporal Coordinate                  | Ordering Mechanism                                    |           Clock Drift Resilience          | Contradiction Handling                     |         Replay Fidelity          |           Storage Overhead           | Query Evaluation Overhead              |     |                  |
|:------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------:|:-------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------:|:------------------------------------:|:---------------------------------------|-----|------------------|
| **Naive Wall-Clock (POSIX)**        | Timestamp ($t_{\text{UTC}}$)         | Total order via local clock                           |       Zero (Vulnerable to NTP skew)       | Destructive Last-Write-Wins (LWW)          |    None (History overwritten)    |      $\mathcal{O}(1)$ base data      | Negligible ($\mathcal{O}(1)$ filter)   |     |                  |
| **Lamport Logical Clocks**          | Monotonic integer $L \in \mathbb{N}$ | Partial causal order ($\max(L, L_{\text{recv}}) + 1$) | Complete (Independent of physical clocks) | Causal precedence; deterministic tie-break |     Weak (Causal order only)     |       $8\text{ B}$ per record        | Low ($\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ index scan) |     |                  |
| **Doyle TMS (Justification Graph)** | Dependency DAG                       | Recursive backtracking                                |     Complete (Logical justifications)     | Strict retraction ($\text{OUT}$ marking)   | Moderate (Retraction edges kept) | High (Explicit justification edges)  | Moderate ($\mathcal{O}(                | E   | )$ verification) |
| **Bi-Temporal Ledger (Snodgrass)**  | 2D plane: $T_V \times T_T$           | Append-only closed intervals                          |     High (Transaction time node-bound)    | Non-destructive interval closure           | Exact (Bit-exact `AS OF` replay) | High ($3\text{--}5\times$ base data) | Low to Moderate (Indexed range scan)   |     |                  |

: **Memory Consistency and Temporal Ordering Paradigms**: Comparison of physical clocks, logical clocks, Truth Maintenance Systems, and bi-temporal ledgers for resolving state contradictions in autonomous agents. {#tbl-vol3-episodic-temporal-paradigms tbl-colwidths="[14,12,14,12,14,12,10,12]"}

## Memory Retrieval Latency and End-to-End SLA {#sec-vol3-episodic-sla}

A financial operations agent is deployed with a contractual Service Level Agreement (SLA) requiring a 99th-percentile (p99) turn response latency below 1,500 milliseconds for every automated portfolio query. The foundation model's autoregressive generation requires 450 ms (Time-to-First-Token prefill of 150 ms plus 300 ms for 20 decode tokens). However, the engineering team designed an unoptimized synchronous memory retrieval pipeline: generating a query embedding via an external REST API takes 380 ms; querying a remote managed vector database across the WAN takes 420 ms; traversing a distributed graph database for entity relations takes 650 ms; and running a cross-encoder re-ranker over 50 retrieved chunks takes 550 ms. Total retrieval overhead alone reaches 2,000 ms. The agent consistently logs a p99 latency of 2,450 ms—blowing past the SLA on 94 percent of production requests and triggering cascading client timeouts.

Building persistent external memory requires enforcing strict systems latency budgets. In an autonomous agent execution loop, memory retrieval sits directly on the critical path between perceiving an environmental observation and emitting the subsequent action. Uncontrolled retrieval latency stalls the agent, drives up operational costs, and violates Service Level Agreements.

### End-to-end turn latency decomposition

The total wall-clock latency of an agent interaction turn ($T_{\text{turn}}$) decomposes into seven sequential phases:

$$T_{\text{turn}} = T_{\text{embed}} + T_{\text{ann}} + T_{\text{graph}} + T_{\text{rerank}} + T_{\text{pack}} + T_{\text{prefill}} + T_{\text{decode}} $$

To satisfy an end-to-end SLA ($T_{\text{turn}} \le T_{\text{SLA}}$), each subsystem must operate within an allocated latency budget.

@Tbl-vol3-episodic-sla-budget details the breakdown between an unoptimized distributed architecture and a production-hardened local-first memory pipeline.

| Subsystem Component                        | Physical Mechanism            |   Unoptimized Distributed Latency    |     Production Local-First Latency    | Critical Systems Bottleneck                 |
|:-------------------------------------------|:------------------------------|:------------------------------------:|:-------------------------------------:|:--------------------------------------------|
| **$T_{\text{embed}}$: Query Embedding**    | Dense encoder forward pass    |   350 – 500 ms (Remote API + WAN)    |    4 – 8 ms (Local TensorRT / ONNX)   | Network RTT & remote queueing               |
| **$T_{\text{ann}}$: Vector Search**        | ANN index traversal           |    250 – 450 ms (Cloud Vector DB)    | 1 – 3 ms (Local IVF-PQ / HNSW in RAM) | Serialization & inter-service network hops  |
| **$T_{\text{graph}}$: Graph Traversal**    | Relational / PPR navigation   |  400 – 700 ms (Multi-hop DB joins)   |   5 – 15 ms (In-memory CSR PageRank)  | Pointer chasing & disk I/O                  |
| **$T_{\text{rerank}}$: Re-Ranking**        | Cross-encoder cross-attention | 400 – 600 ms (Full transformer pass) | 0.1 – 0.5 ms (Reciprocal Rank Fusion) | Quadratic attention compute over candidates |
| **$T_{\text{pack}}$: Context Assembly**    | Knapsack symbol packing       | 20 – 50 ms (Unindexed text parsing)  |  1 – 2 ms (Greedy density selection)  | String manipulation & token counting        |
| **$T_{\text{prefill}}$: Prompt Prefill**   | Foundation model prefill      |   150 – 300 ms (GPU Tensor Cores)    |    150 – 300 ms (GPU Tensor Cores)    | Context bloat ("Retrieval Tax")             |
| **$T_{\text{decode}}$: Generation**        | Autoregressive token decode   | 250 – 400 ms (HBM memory bandwidth)  |  250 – 400 ms (HBM memory bandwidth)  | Memory bandwidth bound                      |
| **Total Turn Latency ($T_{\text{turn}}$)** | End-to-End Interaction Turn   | **1,820 – 3,000 ms (SLA VIOLATION)** |    **411 – 728 ms (SLA COMPLIANT)**   | **Architectural Pipeline Design**           |

: **End-to-End Memory Retrieval and Execution Latency Budget Breakdown**: Contrasting the catastrophic overheads of unoptimized, distributed multi-service memory architectures against production-grade local-first pipelines under a 1,500 ms p99 SLA. {#tbl-vol3-episodic-sla-budget tbl-colwidths="[16,18,18,18,30]"}

### Arithmetic and Roofline analysis of retrieval components

Analyzing the physical rooflines of each retrieval stage reveals why naive architectures collapse:

#### 1. Query embedding latency ($T_{\text{embed}}$)

Invoking an external cloud embedding API incurs Round-Trip Time (RTT) over the WAN, HTTP header serialization, and remote queueing delay:

$$T_{\text{embed, remote}} = 2 \cdot \text{RTT} + T_{\text{TLS}} + T_{\text{queue}} + T_{\text{compute}} \approx 2(40\text{ ms}) + 20\text{ ms} + 150\text{ ms} + 50\text{ ms} = 300\text{ ms} $$

Conversely, deploying a dedicated local small encoder (e.g., a 110M parameter model such as BGE-Small or MiniLM) on a local GPU or CPU host running TensorRT yields:

$$T_{\text{embed, local}} = \frac{2 \cdot N_{\text{tokens}} \cdot P_{\text{embed}}}{P_{\text{peak\_flops}}} \approx \frac{2 \cdot 64 \cdot 1.1 \times 10^8}{5 \times 10^{12}\text{ FLOPS}} \approx 0.0028\text{ s} = 2.8\text{ ms} $$

Local embedding generation achieves a **$100\times$ latency reduction**, transforming an SLA-breaking bottleneck into a negligible fraction of the turn budget.

#### 2. Vector index search latency ($T_{\text{ann}}$)

In an IVF-PQ architecture with ADC, index search consists of two phases:

- Precomputing the distance lookup table $\mathcal{D}$: $256 \cdot D$ arithmetic operations ($\approx 0.05\text{ ms}$).
- Scanning candidate postings lists: Streaming $N_{\text{cand}} = \frac{n_{\text{probe}} N}{K_{\text{ivf}}}$ quantized records of $M$ bytes each across memory buses.

The scan latency is strictly memory-bandwidth bound:

$$T_{\text{scan}} = \frac{N_{\text{cand}} \cdot M}{B_{\text{mem}}} $$

For an episodic store of $N = 10^7$ memories with $K_{\text{ivf}} = 4096$, $n_{\text{probe}} = 32$, and $M = 64$:

$$N_{\text{cand}} = \frac{32 \times 10^7}{4096} \approx 78,125 \text{ vectors} $$

$$\text{Data Volume} = 78,125 \times 64\text{ bytes} \approx 5.0\text{ MB} $$

On host DRAM with $B_{\text{mem}} = 100\text{ GB/s}$:

$$T_{\text{scan}} = \frac{5.0 \times 10^6\text{ bytes}}{10^{11}\text{ bytes/s}} = 0.05\text{ ms} $$

Total vector index search completes in under $0.2\text{ ms}$. Remote vector databases that require JSON-over-HTTP serialization add $200\text{--}400\text{ ms}$ of needless network overhead.

#### 3. Cross-encoder re-ranking vs. reciprocal rank fusion ($T_{\text{rerank}}$)

A common design pitfall is passing the top-100 retrieved candidates into a heavy cross-encoder model for re-ranking. A cross-encoder concatenates the query with each candidate document, computing full self-attention across all tokens:

$$\mathcal{O}(K_{\text{cand}} \cdot (L_q + L_d)^2) $$

Evaluating 100 candidates of 256 tokens each through a 7B-parameter cross-encoder requires tens of trillions of FLOPs, imposing a 400 to 600 ms latency penalty.

Production architectures replace neural cross-encoders with **Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)**\index{Reciprocal Rank Fusion}, an algorithmic scoring function that fuses ranked candidate lists from disparate retrieval modalities (e.g., dense vector search and sparse BM25) without forward-pass computation:

$$\text{RRF\_Score}(d) = \sum_{m \in \mathcal{M}} \frac{1}{k_0 + r_m(d)} $$

where $\mathcal{M} = \{\text{dense}, \text{sparse}, \text{graph}\}$, $r_m(d)$ is the 1-based rank of document $d$ in retrieval modality $m$, and $k_0 \approx 60$ is a smoothing constant that bounds the influence of outlier top ranks.

Listing @lst-vol3-episodic-rrf-fusion implements Reciprocal Rank Fusion.

::: {#lst-vol3-episodic-rrf-fusion lst-cap="**Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)**: Combining rankings from multiple retrieval modalities without neural inference overhead."}
```python
def reciprocal_rank_fusion(
    ranked_lists: list[list[str]],
    k_0: int = 60
) -> list[tuple[str, float]]:
    """Fuse multiple ranked candidate lists into a single consolidated ranking

    using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF). Executes in sub-millisecond time.
    """
    scores: dict[str, float] = {}
    for r_list in ranked_lists:
        for rank, doc_id in enumerate(r_list, start=1):
            scores[doc_id] = scores.get(doc_id, 0.0) + 1.0 / (k_0 + rank)

    # Sort documents descending by aggregated RRF score
    return sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda item: item[1], reverse=True)
```
:::

Evaluating RRF across 500 candidates executes in less than $0.5\text{ ms}$ on a single CPU core, eliminating the cross-encoder bottleneck entirely.

### The prefill retrieval tax

Every memory token injected into an agent's prompt increases the prefill latency of the foundation model. For standard dense self-attention, prefill computation scales quadratically with sequence length $L$.

Let $L_{\text{base}}$ be the baseline prompt length (system prompt, tool schemas, immediate trajectory history), and let $K$ be the number of retrieved memory tokens injected into context. The marginal compute overhead—the **Prefill Retrieval Tax**\index{Prefill Retrieval Tax}—is derived as:

$$\Delta \text{FLOPs} = 2 \cdot n_{\text{layers}} \cdot d_{\text{model}} \cdot \left( (L_{\text{base}} + K)^2 - L_{\text{base}}^2 \right) = 2 \cdot n_{\text{layers}} \cdot d_{\text{model}} \cdot (2 L_{\text{base}} K + K^2) $$

For a 70B parameter model ($n_{\text{layers}} = 80, d_{\text{model}} = 8192$) with a baseline prompt of $L_{\text{base}} = 16,384$ tokens, injecting $K = 8,192$ retrieved memory tokens increases prefill operations by:

$$\Delta \text{FLOPs} = 2 \times 80 \times 8192 \times (2(16384)(8192) + (8192)^2) \approx 1.31 \times 10^6 \times 3.35 \times 10^8 \approx 4.4 \times 10^{14}\text{ FLOPs} $$

On an accelerator delivering $P_{\text{peak}} = 1000\text{ TFLOPS}$ sustained prefill throughput, this injects an additional:

$$\Delta T_{\text{prefill}} = \frac{4.4 \times 10^{14}}{10^{15}} = 440\text{ ms} $$

Injecting 8k tokens of retrieved memory consumes nearly half a second of GPU prefill time, independent of retrieval database speed. Memory systems must practice **Strict Knapsack Packing**: every injected token must justify its prefill latency cost through high relevance density ($p_v^* / \text{cost}(v)$).

### Systems strategies for SLA bounding

Production agent runtimes deploy three systems mechanisms to bound retrieval latency within strict SLAs:

1. **Asynchronous Pre-Fetching:** The runtime does not wait for tool execution to terminate before querying memory. While an external tool executes, the runtime parses streaming stdout, identifies candidate entities, and pre-fetches potential memory records asynchronously. When the tool commits, memory candidates are already warm in host DRAM.
2. **Hard SLA Timeouts and Graceful Fallback:** The retrieval engine enforces a strict timeout (e.g., $T_{\text{retrieval, max}} = 35\text{ ms}$). If a remote knowledge graph or distributed vector partition fails to respond within this deadline, the engine terminates the query and falls back to locally cached scratchpad memory. Proceeding with partial context preserves interactive SLA compliance; blocking indefinitely guarantees an SLA outage.
3. **Prefix Caching of Invariant Episodic Memories:** Frequently accessed episodic summaries (such as weekly architecture invariants or core coding style guides) are pinned at the prefix boundary of the prompt buffer. Serving runtimes (@sec-vol3-virtual-memory) preserve the KV-cache blocks for these invariant prefixes, eliminating prefill computation across turns.

Having examined the physical mechanisms of the memory hierarchy, vector indices, knowledge graphs, offline consolidation, and retrieval latency budgets, we now analyze common architectural fallacies and engineering pitfalls in persistent memory systems.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-vol3-episodic-fallacies}

Designing persistent memory systems for autonomous agents requires navigating subtle trade-offs between retrieval recall, latency, consistency, and physical memory capacity. In the systems tradition established by @hennessy2011computer, this section dismantles common architectural misconceptions.

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy:** *Context windows of 2M+ tokens make external episodic memory architectures obsolete.*

With frontier foundation models expanding supported context windows beyond one million tokens, engineers frequently assume that all state—repository files, multi-week execution logs, terminal outputs, and intermediate scratchpads—can simply be appended to the active prompt, rendering external vector indices, knowledge graphs, and memory consolidation obsolete.

This intuition collapses when evaluated against the physical mechanics of accelerator hardware:

1. **Quadratic Prefill Compute and TTFT:** Ingesting a prompt requires computing full self-attention across the entire sequence length $L$. Prefill compute scales quadratically: $\mathcal{O}(L^2 \cdot d_{\text{model}})$. Ingesting a 1,000,000-token prompt requires over $10^{14}$ floating-point operations before the stochastic processor emits its initial action token. In interactive systems, this imposes a Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) penalty of 15 to 30 seconds, paralyzing closed-loop tool actuation.
2. **High-Bandwidth Memory Saturation:** Key-Value (KV) cache storage scales linearly with sequence length $L$. For a representative 70-billion-parameter model ($n_{\text{layers}} = 80, d_{\text{model}} = 8192$) with Grouped-Query Attention (GQA, 8:1 query-to-KV head ratio) in FP16 precision, storing the KV cache for $L = 10^6$ tokens requires:
   $$M_{\text{KV}} = 2 \times 2 \times 80 \times \left(\frac{8192}{8}\right) \times 10^6 \approx 3.28 \times 10^{11}\text{ bytes} \approx 328\text{ GB} $$
   A single agent trajectory consumes more than four 80 GB NVIDIA H100 GPUs solely to hold its KV cache. Concurrency collapses to zero; no other agent session can run on the node.
3. **Attention Dispersion and "Lost in the Middle":** Transformer attention weights are not uniformly distributed across a million tokens. Empirical studies consistently demonstrate that retrieval fidelity follows a U-shaped curve [@liu2024lost]: facts located in the middle third of expansive contexts suffer from severe recall degradation compared to tokens located at the extreme prefix or suffix.
4. **Economic Compounding:** In an iterative 40-turn trajectory, evaluating an uncompacted 1M-token prompt across every step bills 40 million cumulative prompt tokens for a single task—imposing an unsustainable financial cost.

Context windows are volatile L1 registers; they are not persistent secondary storage. Scaling agent operations mandates multi-tier memory hierarchies.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall:** *Synchronous remote vector and graph database calls in the agent's critical actuation loop.*

In naive agent implementations, the runtime queries external vector databases or remote graph endpoints synchronously on every turn, blocking the local execution thread while waiting for remote network responses.

This pattern incurs severe systems penalties:

1. **Network WAN Latency and Tail Jitter:** While local DRAM lookups complete in nanoseconds and local NVMe reads in microseconds, remote cloud database RPCs incur wide tail-latency distributions ($100\text{--}800\text{ ms}$ at p99). WAN packet loss or remote multi-tenant queueing stalls the agent's control loop.
2. **Accelerator Idle Stranding:** During synchronous remote I/O, the agent's active KV cache remains allocated in GPU HBM. If an agent executes 25 turns with an average remote retrieval wait time of $400\text{ ms}$, the accelerator sits idle for 10 seconds of unutilized HBM allocation, driving down cluster throughput.
3. **Cascading Timeouts:** If an external vector service encounters a transient partition, synchronous retrieval calls time out, crashing the entire agent trajectory midway through a complex task.

Production architectures decouple retrieval from execution: queries are executed against local, embedded in-process indices (such as Faiss or DuckDB) mapped directly into host memory, or pre-fetched asynchronously with strict timeout fallbacks.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy:** *High cosine similarity ($S_C \ge 0.85$) guarantees factual correctness and logical relevance.*

Software developers frequently assume that if an episodic memory search returns a candidate chunk with a cosine similarity exceeding $0.85$, the chunk is logically relevant and safe to inject into the active reasoning prompt.

This assumption fails due to **Polarity Blindness**\index{Polarity Blindness} in dense latent embeddings:

1. **InfoNCE Geometry:** Contrastive embedding models maximize the inner product between topically related texts. Because a statement and its direct negation share identical technical nouns, verbs, and syntax, their embeddings cluster adjacent to one another in latent space.
2. **False Premise Injection:** A query such as *"Is authentication enabled on port 8080?"* will retrieve both *"Authentication is enabled on port 8080"* and *"Authentication is disabled on port 8080"* with virtually identical similarity scores ($S_C > 0.90$). If the system relies solely on similarity thresholds, it injects negated or obsolete facts into the prompt, triggering catastrophic reasoning hallucinations.

Dense vector retrieval must be guarded by symbolic validation layers, temporal validity filters (Truth Maintenance Systems), and deterministic relational predicates.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall:** *The Zombie Memory Trap in long-lived agents.*

In continuous, multi-week agent deployments, episodic vector stores accumulate every raw observation: ephemeral container IDs, temporary debugging ports, transient scratch files, and intermediate error traces. Without an eviction and compaction policy, these stale observations become "Zombie Memories."

Zombie memories degrade systems performance across three dimensions:

1. **Retrieval Precision Dilution:** As millions of transient records flood the index, the nearest-neighbor search returns obsolete scratchpad traces instead of authoritative architectural decisions, diluting context precision.
2. **Stale Configuration Enactment:** An agent attempting to restart a failed service retrieves a temporary port binding from three days earlier, attempts to bind to an allocated port, and crashes.
3. **Memory Footprint Explosion:** Storing millions of uncompressed 1536-dimensional FP32 vectors exhausts host DRAM, forcing indices into swap and multiplying query latency by an order of magnitude.

Mitigating the Zombie Memory Trap requires enforcing strict Time-To-Live (TTL) metadata, bi-temporal interval closing, and offline sleep consolidation cycles to purge transient operational noise.

:::

## Summary {#sec-vol3-episodic-summary}

Episodic and external memory systems transform autonomous agents from stateless, volatile input-output processors into stateful, persistent computational architectures capable of learning across unbounded operational horizons. Just as classical computing systems rely on a memory hierarchy to balance nanosecond register speeds against petabyte storage capacities, scalable agent architectures separate volatile GPU context registers and paged KV caches from non-volatile secondary stores. Operating persistent memory over stochastic processors requires engineering strict transactional boundaries: the Write-Ahead Log invariant ensures that proposed actions are flushed to durable storage before crossing the actuation boundary, protecting against environmental desynchronization during process crashes.

High-dimensional vector indexing provides fast exploratory retrieval over unstructured execution traces, but the curse of dimensionality and polarity blindness prevent dense embeddings from acting as an authoritative truth substrate. Production architectures augment dense Approximate Nearest Neighbor indices (IVF-PQ and HNSW) with structural knowledge graphs derived from Tree-Sitter AST skeletonization and Personalized PageRank, guaranteeing syntactic completeness for deterministic environments. To prevent context poisoning in non-stationary worlds, offline sleep cycles consolidate raw trajectories into compact operational rules, while Doyle's Truth Maintenance Systems and bi-temporal ledgers decouple active planning truth from historical auditability. By bounding retrieval overheads through local-first pipelines, asynchronous pre-fetching, and strict knapsack packing, systems architects ensure that persistent memory enhances reasoning precision without violating interactive Service Level Agreements.

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Episodic and external memory systems"}
1. **The Tripartite Hierarchy Invariant:** Memory must be strictly partitioned into Parametric ($\theta$), Volatile Working Context (GPU HBM / DRAM), and Non-Volatile Secondary Episodic Storage (Disk / NVMe). Context windows are volatile L1 registers; treating them as persistent storage induces quadratic compute bottlenecks, memory exhaustion, and attention dispersion.
2. **The Write-Ahead Log Invariant:** To prevent state divergence upon crash recovery, an agent runtime must enforce the precedence $\text{Log}(s_t, a_t) \prec_{\text{commit}} \text{Execute}(a_t) \prec_{\text{commit}} \text{Log}(o_t, s_{t+1})$. No external tool command may be dispatched until the action proposal has been flushed to non-volatile disk via synchronous storage barriers.
3. **Hybrid Topological Retrieval:** Dense vector retrieval captures thematic affinity but suffers from polarity blindness and syntactic amnesia. Production systems must implement dual-stage pipelines: dense ANN search discovers entry-point seeds, followed by Personalized PageRank over AST symbol graphs to retrieve structurally complete context.
4. **Non-Monotonic Truth Maintenance:** Environmental states are non-stationary. Systems cannot treat historical memories as timeless assertions; they must deploy Doyle Truth Maintenance Systems (marking beliefs $\text{IN}$ or $\text{OUT}$) and bi-temporal schemas ($T_V \times T_T$) to resolve contradictions while preserving bit-exact historical auditability.
5. **Retrieval SLA Governance:** Memory retrieval resides on the critical execution path. To satisfy sub-second SLAs, runtimes must eliminate remote WAN RPCs in favor of local-first indices, replace neural cross-encoders with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, and enforce knapsack token packing to minimize the quadratic Prefill Retrieval Tax.
:::

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From external memory to state checkpointing"}
Episodic memory provides an autonomous agent with durable knowledge, structural environmental representations, and causally ordered belief histories. However, autonomous agency fundamentally involves **environmental mutation**\index{Environmental mutation}. Unlike a closed operating system that merely mutates local disk blocks, an agent's actions trigger external side effects across third-party APIs, distributed cloud databases, and physical infrastructure.

What happens when an agent executes a multi-step workflow that fails mid-flight, leaves half-provisioned cloud resources stranded, or encounters a Byzantine hallucination?

In @sec-vol3-checkpointing (*Trajectory Checkpointing and State Persistence*), we investigate the systems mechanisms required to achieve fault tolerance:

- Formulating the **Fail-Plausible Fault Model**\index{Fail-Plausible Fault Model}, recognizing that stochastic agents fail not by halting, but by hallucinating convincing, invalid execution states.
- Establishing the **Reversibility Boundary**\index{Reversibility Boundary}, formally categorizing actions into reversible local operations versus irreversible external mutations.
- Implementing **Distributed Sagas**\index{Distributed Sagas} and compensating transactions ($A^{-1}$) to unwind failed multi-turn workflows without holding distributed locks.
- Serializing the complete **Agent Control Block (ACB)**\index{Agent Control Block} to enable deterministic point-in-time recovery and time-travel debugging.
:::

## Quantitative Problems {#sec-vol3-episodic-problems}

1. **Vector Memory Footprint and IVF-PQ Compaction Arithmetic:**
   An autonomous fleet of $K = 500$ coding agents operates continuously over a six-month development cycle, accumulating an aggregate episodic history of $N = 5 \times 10^7$ execution memories. Each memory item is represented by an uncompressed dense embedding vector of dimension $D = 1536$ in 32-bit floating-point precision (FP32). Additionally, the memories form an entity dependency graph where each memory item maintains an average of $d_{\text{avg}} = 30$ directed edges to other memories, with each edge represented by an 8-byte integer identifier.
   (a) Calculate the total physical memory footprint (in gigabytes) required to store the raw uncompressed flat vector embeddings and the uncompressed graph edge list in host RAM.
   (b) To reduce memory costs, the engineering team migrates the vector store to an Inverted File Product Quantization (IVF-PQ) architecture with $M = 64$ sub-vectors, where each sub-vector is quantized using an 8-bit codebook ($K_{\text{pq}} = 256$ centroids). Calculate the new memory footprint for the vector index (including the PQ byte codes and the codebook centroids in FP32).
   (c) What is the overall data compression factor achieved for the vector index, and can the combined IVF-PQ index and graph edge list fit into a single memory-optimized server with 256 GB of host RAM?

2. **Personalized PageRank and AST Repomap Knapsack Packing:**
   An agent is tasked with debugging a memory leak in a module containing a symbol dependency graph of $|V| = 20,000$ unique symbols and $|E| = 120,000$ directed dependency edges. The agent's current edit focuses on a seed set of $|\mathcal{S}| = 2$ functions. The runtime executes Personalized PageRank (PPR) using power iteration with a teleport probability of $\alpha = 0.18$.
   (a) In power iteration, the transition matrix multiplication step evaluates $\mathbf{P}^T \mathbf{p}^{(t)}$. Express the number of floating-point operations required per iteration in terms of $|V|$ and $|E|$. How many FLOPs are required to execute 40 iterations?
   (b) After convergence, the top 5 ranked symbols outside the seed set exhibit the following stationary probabilities and Tree-Sitter AST skeleton token costs:

       - Symbol $A$: $p_A^* = 0.045$, $\text{cost}(A) = 350\text{ tokens}$
       - Symbol $B$: $p_B^* = 0.038$, $\text{cost}(B) = 180\text{ tokens}$
       - Symbol $C$: $p_C^* = 0.025$, $\text{cost}(C) = 120\text{ tokens}$
       - Symbol $D$: $p_D^* = 0.020$, $\text{cost}(D) = 220\text{ tokens}$
       - Symbol $E$: $p_E^* = 0.015$, $\text{cost}(E) = 90\text{ tokens}$
       If the agent runtime allocates a strict repomap token budget of $B_{\text{repomap}} = 500\text{ tokens}$, determine which symbols are selected under greedy density knapsack packing ($\text{density} = p_v^* / \text{cost}(v)$). Calculate the total token consumption and the aggregate relevance score packed into context.

3. **End-to-End Latency Budgeting and the Prefill Retrieval Tax:**
   A customer-support agent operates under a strict Service Level Agreement requiring an end-to-end response latency of $T_{\text{SLA}} \le 1,200\text{ ms}$ at p95. The foundation model has 70 billion parameters ($n_{\text{layers}} = 80, d_{\text{model}} = 8192$), and autoregressive generation decodes 25 tokens at a rate of 12 ms per token ($T_{\text{decode}} = 300\text{ ms}$). The baseline prompt context (system prompt, user query, tool schemas) contains $L_{\text{base}} = 8,192\text{ tokens}$. The GPU serving cluster delivers a sustained prefill throughput of $P_{\text{prefill}} = 400\text{ TFLOPS}$ ($4 \times 10^{14}\text{ FLOPs/s}$).
   (a) Calculate the baseline prefill latency $T_{\text{prefill, base}}$ for the $8,192$-token prompt without any retrieved external memory, using the standard prefill FLOP approximation $\text{FLOPs} = 2 \cdot n_{\text{layers}} \cdot d_{\text{model}} \cdot L^2$.
   (b) The retrieval engine uses an unoptimized remote vector database and cross-encoder pipeline that consumes $T_{\text{retrieval}} = 450\text{ ms}$ and retrieves $K = 4,096$ memory tokens. Calculate the new prefill latency $T_{\text{prefill, total}}$ for the expanded prompt ($L_{\text{base}} + K = 12,288\text{ tokens}$). What is the marginal latency cost of the Prefill Retrieval Tax ($\Delta T_{\text{prefill}}$)?
   (c) Calculate the total end-to-end turn latency $T_{\text{turn}} = T_{\text{retrieval}} + T_{\text{prefill, total}} + T_{\text{decode}}$. Does this turn satisfy the $1,200\text{ ms}$ SLA?
   (d) If the engineering team migrates to a local-first memory pipeline that reduces $T_{\text{retrieval}}$ to $15\text{ ms}$ and uses strict knapsack packing to bound retrieved memory to $K = 1,024\text{ tokens}$, re-evaluate $T_{\text{prefill, total}}$ and the new total turn latency $T_{\text{turn}}$. What is the resulting latency margin relative to the SLA?
